slides.title: Architecture and Memory Semantics
slides.subtitle: From XPU transactions to Ethernet transport
slides.transcript:
Scale-Up Ethernet Transport, or SUE-T, connects the memory-transaction interface of an accelerator to an Ethernet scale-up network. An XPU is the generic accelerator in this specification.

You'll follow a transaction through that endpoint and learn what its acknowledgement actually means. That distinction matters when a system reports success before data is visible in memory. This course uses the SUE-T Base Specification, version one point zero point zero. Let's begin with the endpoint's responsibilities.

slides.title: Four Modules from Transactions to Completion
slides.subtitle: Architecture → packet delivery → interface mapping → completion contracts
modules_listed: From XPU Transactions to Ethernet Transport
Efficient Packets on a Lossless Fabric
Map the XPU Interface to the Transport
Define Completion and Evaluate the Design
slides.transcript:
This course follows Scale-Up Ethernet Transport, or SUE-T, through four connected modules. You'll trace a memory transaction, explain packing and ordered recovery, and evaluate the accelerator interface's completion contract.

The first module establishes the architecture and acknowledgement model. The second follows eligible queues into packets and examines the response to a sequence gap. The third maps interface identity, ordering, and request encoding. The fourth compares write-completion choices and applies them to a concrete integration case.

Allow about seventy-five minutes for the narration, worked cases, knowledge checks, and review. The modules have different time budgets because packet recovery and completion decisions need more practice than the initial architecture model.

Begin with one question: what has happened at the destination when the source receives an acknowledgement? We'll build on that distinction throughout the course.

slides.title: The Scale-Up Envelope Has Explicit Conditions
rows: 2–4 · at least two to avoid deadlock
Section 8.4.2 also supports bursts up to 4KB
slides.subtitle: Keep latency, topology, and transaction-size statements in their stated contexts.
slides.transcript:
The scope table gives us the conditions under which to understand the SUE-T architecture. It describes a shared-memory system with up to sixteen thousand accelerators and one-sided load, store, and atomic operations. Memory registration sits outside the transport's scope.

The table specifies an end-to-end round-trip time below two microseconds for a fifteen-hundred-byte packet in a single-hop network. Keep all of those conditions together. The single-hop configuration is central to the design's latency and complexity assumptions. Larger networks are possible, with additional implementation area and complexity.

Traffic is divided into two to four independent traffic classes. At least two are needed because requests and responses must use different classes to avoid deadlock. We'll examine the queue and flow-control consequences in the packet-delivery module.

The same scope table describes a maximum of two hundred fifty-six bytes of data per transaction, with larger operations broken down by the accelerator. Later, the Advanced eXtensible Interface, or AXI, integration section describes support for bursts up to four kilobytes. The relationship between those two statements needs clarification in the specification; we'll keep each in its stated context.

For a design review, ask which topology, packet size, transaction model, and traffic classes the implementation assumes. Those conditions are part of the architectural claim.

slides.title: Separate the XPU, Transport, and Network Layers

figure.alt: SUE-T maps XPU commands above one of three Ethernet network envelopes. Registration and the XPU-specific translation service are external responsibilities.
figure.caption: SUE-T maps XPU commands above one of three Ethernet network envelopes. Registration and the XPU-specific translation service are external responsibilities.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
Start at the top of the stack, where the accelerator issues a memory transaction. SUE-T accepts the transaction through its command interface, maps the control information, and assembles the transport data needed to reach another accelerator.

The transport uses the Unified Local profile of Ultra Ethernet Transport, or UET. Its reliability and semantic layers give the network packet information about the connection, the command, and the associated data.

Below that transport, the specification provides three network options. These are Ethernet for Scale-Up Networks, or ESUN; the Unified Forwarding Header, or UFH; and User Datagram Protocol over Internet Protocol over Ethernet, usually called UDP over IP. The network envelope changes while the transport continues to serve the accelerator's transactions.

This layering also tells us where integration responsibilities belong. Memory registration and protection-domain management are outside SUE-T. Address translation can take place in the command-mapping function or within the accelerator, but the translation service itself is accelerator-specific and outside the transport definition.

The Ethernet fabric provides the service that the transport relies on. SUE-T requires lossless network service, and the packet-delivery module will explain the flow-control and retry choices around that requirement.

When you inspect an implementation, identify these boundaries first: the accelerator's memory system, the transport endpoint, and the network beneath it. Each contributes a different part of the behavior.

slides.title: Multiple Instances Build Aggregate XPU Bandwidth

bullets.text: Example instance: 1.6T with 2×800 Gb/s or 4×400 Gb/s ports.
Example XPU integration: six instances, 9.6 Tb/s aggregate bandwidth.
Instance count and port arrangement are implementation choices.

figure.alt: Example integration from the SUE-T specification; these numbers describe the illustrated arrangement.
figure.caption: Example integration from the SUE-T specification; these numbers describe the illustrated arrangement.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
An accelerator can integrate multiple SUE-T instances. Each instance supplies network connectivity through one or more ports, so the integration can scale aggregate bandwidth by adding transport instances around the accelerator.

The specification gives a concrete example. One instance supports one point six terabits per second using either two eight-hundred-gigabit ports or four four-hundred-gigabit ports. Six such instances provide nine point six terabits per second of aggregate scale-up bandwidth.

Those numbers illustrate an integration arrangement. They don't specify how every accelerator must be built or establish the useful throughput of a particular workload. The example helps explain why instance area, buffering, and state matter: an endpoint design can be replicated several times within the same accelerator.

The later load-balancing discussion distinguishes distributing work across instances from assigning packed work to ports within an instance. For now, keep the deployment picture simple. One accelerator can contain several transport instances, and one transport instance can expose several Ethernet ports.

slides.title: Map, Queue, Pack, Deliver, and Unpack

figure.alt: Command mapping, destination/TC queues, packing, reliability, and receive unpacking form distinct stages.
figure.caption: Command mapping, destination/TC queues, packing, reliability, and receive unpacking form distinct stages.

text_inventory.review_method: Previously reviewed media retained; revised transaction-flow sequence re-timed and decoded checkpoints reviewed after narration correction.

slides.transcript:
Follow a store request through one SUE-T instance. The accelerator supplies the command and its data. The mapping stage assembles them into a command payload data unit, which we'll call a CMD_PDU. Any required address-translation integration happens around this mapping stage.

The transmit buffer places the command into a queue associated with the destination accelerator and traffic class. The buffer reports whether the queue can be serviced, taking account of available space, queued work, and flow-control state. The scheduler selects an eligible queue.

The packing stage reads the available commands from that queue and combines those that fit into a packet payload. A single available command can be sent immediately; the scheduler doesn't wait just to make a fuller packet. We'll examine that rule in the next module.

The reliability layer adds connection information and a packet sequence number, or PSN. The network layer then adds the selected network headers, and the port transmits the packet.

At the destination, the Ethernet and transport checks establish whether the packet can be accepted. For this example, assume the expected sequence number arrives. The receiver buffers the payload, separates it into individual command payload data units, maps their fields to the local command interface, and passes them to the receiving accelerator.

We've now followed delivery through the endpoint. The timing and meaning of the acknowledgement still depend on the selected acknowledgement mode. A command reaching the destination interface and a memory operation completing are separate events to track.

slides.title: A Delivery ACK and an Operational ACK Mean Different Things

figure.alt: Delivery ACK confirms delivery; Operational ACK associates the XPU response with the request. Data and errors still need their response information.
figure.caption: Delivery ACK confirms delivery; Operational ACK associates the XPU response with the request. Data and errors still need their response information.

entries.text: Delivery ACK does not generate the source XPU response
Operational ACK waits for the destination XPU response
Source reconstructs the XPU success responses
Memory visibility depends on the completion contract

text_inventory.review_method: Previously reviewed media retained; revised transaction-flow sequence re-timed and decoded checkpoints reviewed after narration correction.

slides.transcript:
Compare two ways to acknowledge the same successful store. Begin with Delivery ACK mode. The source sends a request, and the remote SUE-T delivers it to the destination accelerator. The delivery acknowledgement returns for that request packet.

That ACK does not generate the response expected by the source's command interface. The destination accelerator produces its own response, which SUE-T transports back as a separate command. That response packet has its own sequence number and is itself acknowledged. The accelerator interface associates the returned response with the original request.

Now start the comparison again in Operational ACK mode. Here, SUE-T retains command state so it can associate the destination's response with the outstanding request. The destination transport waits for the accelerator responses for all commands in that packet before acknowledging the packet.

Suppose every operation succeeds and none returns data. The destination can communicate those results through the acknowledged packet sequence number. The source transport uses its retained state to generate the corresponding success responses for the local command interface. This exchanges more local state for less response information carried over the wire.

In Operational ACK mode, data-bearing responses and error responses need dedicated acknowledgement packets. A load, for example, still needs its returned data. Operational acknowledgement doesn't remove that information requirement.

The comparison gives us two useful questions. Has the command been delivered, and has the destination produced the operation's response? Neither question, by itself, defines when every other observer can see data in memory. For that, we also need the completion and global-observability contract.

slides.title: Completion and Global Observability Are Separate Decisions

bullets.text: Delivery, XPU response, and memory placement are distinct events.
When supported and requested, global observability holds the XPU response until data is placed.
Either ACK mode can support global observability.

figure.alt: Read the acknowledgement together with the response and memory-visibility contract.
figure.caption: Read the acknowledgement together with the response and memory-visibility contract.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
An acknowledgement is useful only when we understand the event it confirms. SUE-T uses one-sided memory semantics: the source controls the operation without needing awareness of a destination process. The receiving accelerator still processes the command, and the source still needs the defined completion behavior.

Delivery ACK mode confirms that the command reached the destination accelerator. Operational ACK mode associates the accelerator's response with the request. The point at which that accelerator response is produced remains important.

Consider a write that has entered a queue on its way to memory. Accepting the write into that queue and placing its data in memory are different events. An implementation may use a completion contract that responds before memory placement. The completion module will compare the alternatives and their error-reporting consequences.

Global observability addresses the memory-placement requirement. When that capability is supported, the accelerator can request it through the command's global-observability control field. The accelerator then holds its response until the data has been placed. The specification allows global observability with either acknowledgement mode.

That means the mode name alone is insufficient. Ask which event produces the accelerator response, whether global observability is supported, and whether the command requests it. These questions connect the transport's acknowledgement to the memory behavior the application actually relies on.

The system also needs registration and protection arrangements outside SUE-T. Transporting a memory command doesn't settle those integration responsibilities.

slides.title: Unified Local Carries the Memory Operations
rows: nop, write, read, atomic, fetching atomic
slides.subtitle: Transaction semantics remain distinct from packet reliability and network headers.
slides.transcript:
The semantic layer tells the receiver what the transported memory operation means. SUE-T uses the Unified Local profile of UET to represent requests and their associated responses. The defined request operations include a no-operation command, writes, reads, atomics, and fetching atomics. Implementations can also use the reserved vendor-defined operation range.

The request header has a twelve-byte form and a compressed eight-byte form. The compressed variant carries a thirty-two-bit address offset relative to the previous address. That preceding address context is part of how the smaller representation works. We'll examine specific compression constraints when we reach AXI integration.

A request can carry up to sixteen bytes of additional accelerator-specific state. The profile also allows up to sixteen transactions to be packed into one packet. Each transaction keeps its semantic information even when several share the same packet.

The response format uses eight bytes of response state per transaction, and up to sixteen responses can be packed into an acknowledgement packet. A response can carry data, or use a zero payload length when there is no data. Its return code distinguishes success from the defined error cases.

Keep the transaction header separate from the packet's reliability header and network envelope. Compression, packing, and acknowledgement choices affect different parts of the wire representation. Understanding those layers will help you compare efficiency without confusing a smaller header with a different memory operation.

slides.title: Keep the Endpoint and Completion Boundaries Clear
items: Use the numerical scope with its single-hop and packet-size conditions.
Keep XPU integration, transport, and network responsibilities distinct.
Trace commands through mapping, queues, packing, and receive unpacking.
Read ACK mode together with the XPU response contract.
Request supported global observability when memory placement is required.
slides.transcript:
You now have the architecture model needed for the rest of the course. SUE-T maps accelerator memory transactions into transport packets and back again. Its scope favors a low-latency single-hop fabric, and its stated numerical conditions belong with that deployment context.

The command interface, transport instance, and Ethernet network each have distinct responsibilities. Registration, protection-domain management, and the accelerator-specific address-translation service need their own integration arrangements.

Delivery ACK confirms delivery to the destination accelerator. Operational ACK associates the destination response with the outstanding command, using local state to reduce response information on the wire where the operation allows it.

Finally, memory visibility depends on the completion contract and, when supported and requested, global observability. Carry that distinction forward. It will help you explain both the reliability choices in the packet path and the write-completion choices at the accelerator interface.

slides.transcript:
Take a moment to check the transaction model. The first question asks what a Delivery ACK establishes. The second asks you to identify the system's responsibilities and the condition associated with global observability.

Submit both questions once to continue. Correct answers aren't required, and you can retry after reading the feedback. Use the explanation to connect your choice to a specific event: command delivery, an accelerator response, or data placement in memory. Those events help define the behavior that a SUE-T implementation must make clear.

slides.title: Packing and Reliable Delivery
slides.subtitle: Efficient packets on a lossless fabric
slides.transcript:
Scale-Up Ethernet Transport, or SUE-T, turns accelerator transactions into packets while balancing latency, wire efficiency, and endpoint state. This module follows that packet path from an eligible transmit queue to ordered delivery at the receiver.

You'll predict when the scheduler should transmit, trace the effect of a missing packet, and compare transport retransmission with the required lossless network service. These distinctions help you evaluate the buffering and resilience choices in an implementation.

slides.title: Follow the Queue, Packet, and Connection
slides.subtitle: Queue eligibility → opportunistic packing → ordered acceptance and recovery
slides.transcript:
We'll connect three parts of the packet-delivery model. The first is the queue: which destination and traffic class own the work, and when is that queue eligible? The second is the packet: which available commands fit together, and what limits constrain packing? The third is the connection: which sequence number does the receiver expect, and what happens if it doesn't arrive?

Two short cases will ask you to predict behavior before the explanation. One involves an eligible queue with only one command. The other involves a packet missing from an ordered sequence. We'll finish with connection scaling and load distribution. Throughout, keep the request and its response separate from the packet that happens to carry them.
objectives: Apply work-conserving packing and packet-size limits.
Trace ordered acceptance and recovery across a sequence gap.
Compare lossless service, link retry, and transport retransmission.

slides.title: Requests and Responses Need Separate Traffic Classes

bullets.text: Queue identity: {destination XPU, traffic class}.
At least two TCs for a VC: requests and responses use different classes.
Dedicated N×K queues or fewer dynamically allocated resources.
Per-TC flow control protects the endpoint buffer.

figure.alt: Destination queues are distinct; request and response traffic classes preserve the required separation.
figure.caption: Destination queues are distinct; request and response traffic classes preserve the required separation.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
A transmit queue belongs to a destination accelerator and a traffic class. That pairing lets the implementation keep work for different destinations and traffic classes distinct as it selects the next packet.

The specification requires at least two traffic classes for one virtual connection. Requests and responses must use different classes to avoid deadlock. A system that also distinguishes higher and lower transaction priorities can require more than two. This is a functional separation to preserve progress, so don't treat the traffic classes as optional labels that can all be collapsed into one queue.

Queue storage can be organized in different ways. With N accelerators and K traffic classes, an implementation may provide N times K dedicated queues. Alternatively, it may allocate fewer queues dynamically to reduce area. The smaller arrangement can experience blocking when the workload spreads small messages across many destinations.

Flow control acts per traffic class. It also matters when the accelerator's command interface can supply work faster than the Ethernet interface transmits it. That mismatch can build up commands in the transmit buffer without any deliberate waiting for packing.

For a design review, separate three questions. Are requests and responses assigned to different traffic classes? How are destination queues allocated? And what makes a queued command eligible for service? The specification fixes the required traffic separation, while leaving queue organization and scheduling discipline to the implementation.

slides.title: Pack Available Work Without Waiting

figure.alt: The example services A, B, C+E, then D. An eligible singleton is sent without waiting to fill a packet.
figure.caption: The example services A, B, C+E, then D. An eligible singleton is sent without waiting to fill a packet.

entries.text: Figure 6 example · service order A, B, C+E, D
Request / response classes remain separate · packet limits still apply
Packing opportunity comes from available work

text_inventory.review_method: Previously reviewed media retained; revised transaction-flow sequence re-timed and decoded checkpoints reviewed after narration correction.

slides.transcript:
Watch the scheduler service the five transactions in the specification's example. A and B are in separate queues. C and E share one destination-and-traffic-class queue. D is in another queue.

The first eligible queue contains A. A leaves in its own packet. The scheduler doesn't keep A waiting for another transaction to arrive. It then services the queue containing B, which also leaves by itself.

When the scheduler selects the queue containing C, E is already available in that same queue. The packing stage can include both C and E in one packet, provided the configured command and payload limits are satisfied. The scheduler then services the queue containing D.

The illustrated service order is A, B, C with E, then D. That order explains the example; it doesn't prescribe a single scheduler algorithm for every implementation. The system designer selects the scheduling discipline, subject to the requirement that it be work conserving.

Now consider a distinct case. One destination queue is eligible and contains a single command. There is no second command ready to pack with it. Predict what should happen. The command is transmitted. Waiting only to improve packing would violate the stated rule that transactions aren't delayed for packing.

Packing is therefore an opportunity created by available work. It can improve efficiency when several commands are queued, including when the accelerator interface supplies them faster than the port can send. Eligibility, flow control, and the configured limits still determine what can leave. There is no invented packet-fill timer in this model.

slides.title: Decide When the Singleton Should Leave

cards.title: Scenario 1
cards.body: One queued store; queue eligible; port ready.

cards.title: Scenario 2
cards.body: Flow control prevents that queue from transmitting.

cards.title: Scenario 3
cards.body: Available commands exceed the configured packet limit.

slides.subtitle: Predict what can transmit in each case. Pause the narration to decide, then resume.
slides.transcript:
Put the rule to work. An eligible destination queue contains one store command. The port can transmit it, and the relevant flow-control conditions allow service. A second command for that destination may arrive later, but it hasn't arrived yet.

Should the scheduler hold the first command to improve wire efficiency? Decide before continuing the explanation. The specification says a single transaction in a selected destination queue is sent. Transactions aren't delayed for packing. A possible future packing partner is not a reason to keep currently eligible work waiting.

Now change one condition. Flow control prevents service of that queue. The work must wait until the queue becomes eligible. That waiting has a defined cause: flow control. If additional commands arrive while it waits, the packing stage may later find several ready together. Their accumulation does not turn the original wait into a packing policy.

Finally, suppose several commands are available but together exceed a configured packet limit. The scheduler can transmit the commands that fit. It cannot ignore the limit merely because a larger group would amortize headers more efficiently.

The useful diagnostic is to name the cause of waiting. Queue eligibility, buffer constraints, flow-control state, and scheduling among eligible work belong in that explanation. Waiting solely for a fuller packet does not. This gives you a concrete way to distinguish a latency-preserving packing implementation from a batching assumption that the specification does not make.

slides.title: Packing Has Command and Payload Limits
slides.transcript:
Packing combines transaction representations within one packet. Each command retains the semantic information needed to describe its operation, address, and associated data. The packet then carries the reliability information that applies to that packed group.

The packing limit is up to sixteen command payload data units. There are also configured payload limits: two K, four K, or eight K for the sum of store and atomic data, and corresponding limits for the sum of load and fetching-atomic response data. A group must satisfy the applicable limits together. Counting commands alone is insufficient when they carry different amounts of data.

The request semantics can use a twelve-byte header or a compressed eight-byte form. The profile can carry up to sixteen bytes of extra accelerator-specific state per transaction. Response state uses eight bytes per transaction. Those transaction-level quantities are separate from the eight-byte reliability header used by Reliable Ordered Delivery for Local networks, or RODL around the packet.

During packing, the semantic headers are updated to represent the packed messages and any address compression. The receive path then separates the packet payload into individual command units for delivery to the accelerator.

More buffering can create more opportunities to find commands ready together, but it consumes area. Buffer sizing also changes when retransmission is enabled because outstanding work must be retained until it is acknowledged. Keep the accounting units clear: command data, per-command semantic state, packed payload, and packet headers. That distinction makes an efficiency comparison much easier to audit.

slides.title: A PDC Holds the Ordered Connection State

bullets.text: PDC: a tracked packet-delivery connection.
State includes next PSN, acknowledged PSN, and timeout state.
Queue/PDCID allocation is implementation-specific.
Dedicated, reserved, or dynamically assigned contexts.

figure.alt: A queue is associated with a delivery context; connection state tracks the packet sequence rather than defining a global memory order.
figure.caption: A queue is associated with a delivery context; connection state tracks the packet sequence rather than defining a global memory order.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
Reliable Ordered Delivery for Local networks, abbreviated RODL, keeps delivery ordered within its connection. That connection is represented by a Packet Delivery Context, or PDC. Its identifier is the PDC identifier.

The context holds state such as the next packet sequence number, the acknowledged sequence number, and timeout information. This is packet-delivery state. A command's address and opcode still belong to its semantic representation, and the accelerator's operation response still has the meaning established by its acknowledgement and completion modes.

The transmit queues are organized by destination accelerator and traffic class, with queues associated with delivery contexts. How the implementation allocates context identifiers and associates them with those queues is implementation-specific.

In a smaller system, it may be practical to maintain a dedicated context for each destination-and-traffic-class pairing. The context identifier might be derived directly from that pairing. In a larger system, fewer contexts can be assigned dynamically to reduce the state that must exist simultaneously. Reserved contexts can also be configured as static connections.

The ordering guarantee belongs to the connection being tracked. It should not be promoted into a global ordering guarantee across all traffic, all ports, or all memory operations. Later, the AXI interface module will show a particularly important boundary: reads and writes have separate ordering rules even when they use the same interface identifier.

For now, identify which packet stream a context describes, how its state is allocated, and which queue uses it. Those questions connect the abstract reliability protocol to the endpoint's storage requirements.

slides.title: A Sequence Gap Changes What the Receiver Accepts

figure.alt: With retransmission enabled, a missing expected packet blocks acceptance of later packets until recovery restores the sequence.
figure.caption: With retransmission enabled, a missing expected packet blocks acceptance of later packets until recovery restores the sequence.

entries.text: Ordered acceptance follows the expected PSN
NACK · do not deliver unexpected packets
GoBackN replays from the missing point: 101, then 102, then 103
Sequence restored · numerical values and spacing are illustrative
Removing transport retry saves state; packet loss is fatal

text_inventory.review_method: Previously reviewed media retained; revised transaction-flow sequence re-timed and decoded checkpoints reviewed after narration correction.

slides.transcript:
Follow one illustrative connection with transport retransmission enabled. Its source sends packets numbered one hundred, one hundred one, one hundred two, and one hundred three. The receiver begins by expecting one hundred.

Packet one hundred arrives and is accepted. The expected sequence advances to one hundred one. Now suppose packet one hundred one is lost. The next packet to arrive is one hundred two. The receiver is still expecting one hundred one, so it doesn't deliver the commands in one hundred two. It sends a negative acknowledgement, or NACK.

Packet one hundred three then arrives while the gap remains. It is also dropped. The specification describes dropping subsequent arrivals from that source until the expected packet arrives. Our example follows one connection, so there is no ambiguity about which sequence is being tracked.

With GoBackN retransmission enabled, the source can replay from the missing point. One hundred one is received and accepted. Replayed packets one hundred two and one hundred three can then be accepted in order. The later commands waited for recovery even though their first packet copies reached the receiver.

The sequence numbers and event spacing in this example are illustrative. They don't define the wire value of a NACK or a fixed timeout. The important behavior is expected-sequence acceptance followed by recovery of the gap.

Now compare an implementation without transport retransmission. Removing retransmission reduces buffer and state requirements, but a lost packet is fatal to the connection. Link-layer retry can make that choice reasonable in some networks; it does not turn a lost transport packet into a successful operation. Lossless network service remains required in either design.

slides.title: Explain What Happens After Packet 101 Is Lost

cards.title: Expected 101; received 102
cards.body: Can these commands be delivered now?

cards.title: Transport retry enabled
cards.body: What buffer and state are needed for recovery?

cards.title: Transport retry disabled
cards.body: What is the consequence of this lost packet?

slides.subtitle: Predict acceptance and recovery before the explanation.
slides.transcript:
The receiver has accepted packet one hundred. Packet one hundred one is missing, and packet one hundred two arrives. Decide whether the commands in one hundred two can be delivered to the accelerator now.

They cannot. RODL is an ordered service. The receiver expects one hundred one and sends a NACK when one hundred two arrives unexpectedly. Subsequent arrivals are dropped until the expected packet arrives. Receiving bytes on the link is different from accepting their commands for delivery.

Next, explain what the implementation needs if transport retransmission is enabled. The source retains unacknowledged command data and the relevant delivery state. Its buffering has to cover the round trip and remote processing time. GoBackN can replay from the missing point, after which the receiver accepts the sequence in order.

Now remove transport retransmission from the design. That saves endpoint state and buffering. It also changes the failure consequence: the lost packet is fatal to the connection. The implementation cannot simply deliver later packets out of order to bypass the gap under this protocol.

Finally, ask whether a lossless fabric makes the transport choice irrelevant. It doesn't remove the specified consequence of a packet that is actually lost. Flow control aims to provide lossless service, and link-layer retry addresses failures at the link. The transport's recovery option remains a distinct part of the endpoint contract.

Explain flow control, link retry, and transport recovery separately. Then use the specified failure consequence to evaluate the implementation.

slides.title: Lossless Service and Retry Solve Different Problems

cards.title: Lossless service
cards.body: PFC or CBFC on all SUE-T traffic classes.

cards.title: Link-layer retry
cards.body: LLR addresses retry at the link layer.

cards.title: Optional transport replay
cards.body: GoBackN needs retained buffers and delivery state.

cards.title: No transport replay
cards.body: Smaller endpoint; packet loss is fatal to the connection.

slides.transcript:
SUE-T requires lossless network service on all of its traffic classes. The specification uses Priority Flow Control, or PFC, or credit-based flow control, or CBFC, to provide that service. Their role is to control traffic so the fabric can preserve the required delivery behavior.

Link Layer Retransmission, or LLR, operates at the link. Transport retransmission operates at the packet-delivery connection. The specification permits removing transport retransmission in a compact endpoint, with the explicit tradeoff that a lost packet becomes fatal to the connection. Keeping GoBackN adds buffering and state but enables transport recovery.

The costs differ. A retransmission-enabled source holds command data until acknowledgement and sizes its buffer for round trip and remote processing time. A lossless fabric must maintain service for every SUE-T traffic class. These requirements should be evaluated together rather than collapsed into a single reliability checkbox.

The document also marks boundaries for future work. Congestion control is not required for its single-switch-hop network model. Multi-tier scale-up congestion-control mechanisms are discussed as possible extensions and left for future work. Multi-port failover is likewise a future-work concept.

Those statements matter in procurement and design reviews. An implementation can offer additional mechanisms, but they need their own documented behavior. The base specification's discussion of future work is not evidence that automatic failover or a complete multi-tier congestion-control solution is already provided by every SUE-T endpoint.

slides.title: Scale Connections and Distribute Traffic Deliberately

bullets.text: Distribute work across instances in software or XPU hardware.
Within a multi-port instance, assign packed groups by available bandwidth.
Example dynamic scale: 1K PDCs for 8K XPUs.
Port-failure failover remains future work in this base specification.

figure.alt: Across-instance distribution and within-instance port assignment are separate design choices.
figure.caption: Across-instance distribution and within-instance port assignment are separate design choices.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
Scaling endpoint bandwidth and scaling connection state are related design choices, but they are different resources. A system may integrate several SUE-T instances around one accelerator. Work can be distributed among those instances in software or by a hardware load-balancing block in the accelerator.

Each instance can provide congestion state to support that distribution. Within an instance that has two or more ports, packed groups of operations can be assigned to ports according to available bandwidth. Across-instance distribution and within-instance port assignment are therefore two distinct levels of balancing.

Connection state also needs to scale. Keeping a dedicated delivery context for every destination-and-traffic-class pairing can be practical in smaller systems. A larger design may assign fewer contexts dynamically. The specification gives the example of one thousand delivery contexts serving eight thousand accelerators.

That example describes a state-saving choice. It doesn't specify a universal context count, a workload-independent throughput result, or a fixed allocation algorithm. A dynamically allocated resource can create blocking under some highly distributed small-message patterns, so traffic distribution matters to the evaluation.

Finally, retain the future-work boundary. The document discusses moving a connection to another port after a port failure as a possible resiliency enhancement, but leaves the concept for future work. Load distribution across available ports is not itself a promise of automatic failure recovery.

For an implementation review, ask where work is distributed, how contexts are allocated, and how failures are handled. Those answers make the bandwidth, state, and resilience claims concrete.

slides.title: Preserve Latency While Choosing State and Resilience
items: Separate request and response traffic classes.
Send eligible singletons; pack only the available work that fits.
Use PDC/PSN state to explain ordered acceptance.
Account for the buffer/state cost of optional GoBackN.
Require lossless service and preserve future-work boundaries.
slides.transcript:
The packet path gives you a practical set of implementation questions. Requests and responses need separate traffic classes. Destination queues can be dedicated or dynamically allocated, with different area and blocking implications.

Packing uses eligible work already available in the selected queue. The scheduler sends a singleton and respects the configured command and payload limits. It doesn't wait solely to fill a packet.

A delivery context tracks an ordered packet stream. An unexpected sequence number creates a gap that later arrivals cannot bypass. Optional GoBackN adds retained buffers and state for recovery; without transport retransmission, packet loss is fatal to the connection.

Lossless service, link-layer retry, and transport replay have distinct jobs. Keep those mechanisms separate when evaluating scale, load distribution, and resilience. That distinction is the foundation for the interface and completion decisions in the final two modules.

slides.transcript:
Check the rules you would use in an implementation review. The first question asks what should happen when an eligible queue has one transaction. The second asks you to classify the consequences of retransmission, lossless service, and ordered receive.

Submit both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry after the feedback. Use each explanation to name the mechanism involved: scheduling, flow control, connection state, or transport recovery. That is more useful than treating all of them as one reliability feature.

slides.title: Evaluate the Packet Path
slides.transcript:
You've completed the packing and reliable-delivery module. You can now predict when queued work should leave and explain why a sequence gap changes what the receiver accepts.

Module three connects those transport behaviors to the accelerator interface. You'll examine Advanced eXtensible Interface, or AXI, mapping, ordering, and request encoding. The final module then applies those facts to write completion, visibility, and error reporting. Use the LMS syllabus to continue with interface mapping.

slides.title: Map the XPU Interface to the Transport
slides.subtitle: Interface roles, identity, ordering, and encoding
slides.transcript:
The accelerator interface determines how application transactions become Scale-Up Ethernet Transport commands, or SUE-T commands. In this module, you'll map interface identity and application state, then separate the ordering guarantees from the packet representation.

We'll compare the signal interface and Advanced eXtensible Interface, or AXI, examples, examine the network envelopes, and apply the specific length and compression constraints. The next module uses those facts to evaluate completion, visibility, and error handling. Begin by identifying the three interfaces around one transport instance.

slides.title: Map the Interface, Then Define Completion
slides.subtitle: Map the interface → define completion → apply the integration case
slides.transcript:
The remaining two modules connect interface mapping to completion. This module explains how the accelerator identifies a destination, carries application-specific information, and represents requests on the wire. You'll also see what ordering is and isn't guaranteed by the AxID.

The next module examines completion. We'll compare four alternative points at which a write may be reported complete, then apply those choices to a concrete write-and-read case.

Keep the questions connected. A correctly encoded packet doesn't settle the memory-ordering contract. An operation response doesn't always establish observer-visible memory placement. Integration requires you to define both the representation and the event that the response confirms. The specification provides the constraints and examples; the implementation makes several of the choices.
objectives: Map the command, management, and network interfaces.
Carry identity and configured opaque application state.
Apply AXI length and compression limits before choosing completion.

slides.title: Command, Management, and Ethernet Have Different Roles

figure.alt: The command, management, and Ethernet interfaces have distinct responsibilities. Optional management-packet transport is unreliable.
figure.caption: The command, management, and Ethernet interfaces have distinct responsibilities. Optional management-packet transport is unreliable.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
A SUE-T instance exposes three interfaces. The command interface carries the accelerator's transactions and associated data. The management interface configures and queries the instance. The Ethernet interface carries the network traffic.

The command protocol can be adapted to the accelerator architecture. The specification supplies two examples: a signal interface built around a FIFO and credits, and an AXI four interface. Integration can use those examples directly or adapt them to the system's needs.

Management is implementation-specific. An AXI target interface is one example of how configuration and status registers may be accessed, but the specification doesn't prescribe a universal register map.

The management path can also offer full-packet transmission and reception. In that option, the accelerator constructs the packet and triggers transmission; SUE-T adds the Ethernet frame check sequence. Received control packets enter a buffer that the accelerator can query. The document explicitly describes this control packet transport as unreliable.

Separately, the optional low-rate control channel supports messages for diagnostics and basic queries. Keep its optional status and limited role clear when evaluating an implementation.

These interfaces serve different decisions. Use the command interface to review transaction semantics and backpressure. Use management to review configuration and status behavior. Use the network interface to review encapsulation and the required fabric service. A management-packet feature should not be mistaken for the reliable memory-transaction path.

slides.title: The Same Transport Uses Three Network Envelopes

figure.alt: ESUN, UFH-16b, and Ethernet/IP/UDP wrap the UET transport differently; identification depends on the selected format.
figure.caption: ESUN, UFH-16b, and Ethernet/IP/UDP wrap the UET transport differently; identification depends on the selected format.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
SUE-T can run over three Ethernet network envelopes. These are Ethernet for Scale-Up Networks, or ESUN, the Unified Forwarding Header or UFH, and User Datagram Protocol, or UDP, over Internet Protocol, or IP, over Ethernet. The transport semantics remain above the chosen network format.

The destination network address is typically configured in the transport instance and looked up from information supplied by the accelerator. A destination accelerator identifier can, for example, select the destination media-access-control, or MAC, address or IP address. In the UFH case, that identifier may be used directly.

The receiver also needs to recognize the transport. For UDP over IP, the specification identifies Ultra Ethernet through destination port four seven nine three. It also gives EtherType hexadecimal E seven nine zero as identifying Ultra Ethernet in the described EtherType case.

With ESUN, the presence of the Ultra Ethernet transport is inferred through network-wide configuration. That is a configuration assumption that the system has to establish consistently.

Within the transport header, the packet-delivery type field identifies the selected Ultra Ethernet Transport, or UET, type, such as Reliable Ordered Delivery for Local networks, or RODL. Network identification and packet-delivery selection therefore answer different questions.

When integrating an endpoint, verify the selected envelope, the mapping from the accelerator identifier to network addressing, and the receive-side identification rule. The three source diagrams are useful precisely because they show the same transport payload carried inside different network headers.

slides.title: A Credit-Based Signal Interface Adapts to the XPU

bullets.text: FIFO-like command/data path with credits.
Flow control per {destination, VC} and aggregate rate.
Control width M and data width N are implementation-specific.
Example N=256 bits: 32B per cycle, eight cycles for 256B.
TX/RX directions and exact fields are in Tables 2–3.

figure.alt: A command and serialized data cross the interface only under the defined credit conditions.
figure.caption: A command and serialized data cross the interface only under the defined credit conditions.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
The signal-interface example is a FIFO-like command path using credits. The accelerator writes a command and any associated data, while SUE-T provides flow control per destination and virtual channel and on an aggregate-rate basis.

Some widths are fixed in the example, and others are implementation-specific. The transmit cycle field is four bits. The operation-valid field and virtual-channel field are two bits each. The remote accelerator identifier is ten to sixteen bits, supporting the stated one-thousand-to-sixteen-thousand accelerator range. The control width and data width depend on the implementation.

The data-width example makes that last point concrete. If the data bus is two hundred fifty-six bits wide, each cycle carries thirty-two bytes. Eight cycles carry two hundred fifty-six bytes. Changing the bus width changes the serialization choices; the example is not a required width for every design.

The transmit table also includes an error signal, credit information, and reset signals. The receive table gives the corresponding commands and data flowing back toward the accelerator, with its own signal directions. Read each direction explicitly rather than assuming every transmit field has an identical receive counterpart.

The complete tables remain available through the source link. For the integration model, concentrate on what the endpoint must know: which destination and virtual channel own the command, what operation and data it carries, and whether enough credits exist to transfer it. Those are the fields that connect a local interface transaction to the transport's queued work.

slides.title: Map Identity and Carry Opaque Application State
rows: Up to 16 bits; reversible AxID ↔ PDCID mapping
0, 32, 64, or 128 used bits; opaque to SUE-T
Configured explicitly; not conveyed by the AXI interface
Contiguous enabled-byte range; otherwise local error
slides.transcript:
The AXI example gives the integrator a specific mapping task. AXI, spoken AXI, is the Advanced eXtensible Interface used here for read and write transactions. The SUE-T interface provides a simplified AXI four mapping with additional semantic information carried through user fields.

The address signal is sixty bits. The AxID can use up to sixteen bits, with the used width configured for the implementation. It represents accelerator identity and connection selection in this mapping. On the send side it maps to a packet-delivery-context identifier. The mapping is reversible, so receive-side connection state can recover the interface identifier without carrying it in the semantic header.

The AxUSER signal has a maximum width of one hundred twenty-eight bits, with supported used sizes of zero, thirty-two, sixty-four, or one hundred twenty-eight. Its contents are opaque to SUE-T. The integrator constructs and deconstructs the application-specific information, and explicitly configures how many bits are used. The interface does not convey that width automatically.

Write strobes have a constraint of their own. The supported enabled bytes must form a contiguous range. A noncontiguous write-strobe pattern is a local error. This lets the remote write representation use a base address and length without carrying an arbitrary strobe mask.

These fields establish address, identity, opaque application state, and a valid write shape. Ordering is another question, which we'll examine separately next.

slides.title: AxID Orders Reads and Writes Separately

figure.alt: Same-AxID reads and writes each preserve their own order. Cross-read/write and cross-AxID ordering are not guaranteed.
figure.caption: Same-AxID reads and writes each preserve their own order. Cross-read/write and cross-AxID ordering are not guaranteed.

entries.text: Illustrative AxID A · separate read and write ordering
Each same-AxID lane preserves its own order
Neither field alone defines global memory visibility

text_inventory.review_method: Previously reviewed media retained; revised transaction-flow sequence re-timed and decoded checkpoints reviewed after narration correction.

slides.transcript:
A shared AxID does not establish one total order across all operations. Follow one illustrative identifier with two writes and two reads.

The writes using that identifier are ordered with respect to each other. The reads using that identifier are also ordered with respect to each other. Those are two separate guarantees: write order and read order.

Now compare a write and a read that use the same identifier. The specification does not guarantee their ordering relative to each other. A read that appears later in an application's intended sequence cannot rely on the identifier alone to establish a dependency on that write.

Next, introduce a different identifier. There is no guaranteed ordering across different identifiers either. The animation uses one permitted illustrative arrangement to make these boundaries visible. It doesn't prescribe a reordering algorithm or say that the implementation must choose that particular schedule.

Before continuing, decide what can be concluded from the identifier. You can conclude the defined same-identifier order within reads and within writes. You cannot infer cross-read/write order, cross-identifier order, or global memory visibility from that identifier alone.

The distinction is especially important after learning about ordered packet delivery. RODL orders the packet stream tracked by its connection. That statement doesn't replace the separately defined AXI ordering rules or choose a write-completion point. Packet acceptance, interface ordering, and memory visibility each need their own contract.

For an integration review, identify the guarantee the application actually needs and the mechanism that provides it. Avoid filling a missing dependency with an assumption about a familiar field name.

slides.title: AXI Length and Compression Have Specific Boundaries

figure.alt: 4096B and a changed extension-header length require ac=0. The burst must also respect the 4KB address boundary.
figure.caption: 4096B and a changed extension-header length require ac=0. The burst must also respect the 4KB address boundary.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
The AXI integration section supports burst transactions up to four kilobytes. A transaction must not cross a four-kilobyte page multiple. That address-boundary rule applies alongside the payload-length rule.

The wire format also has a compression boundary. The extended write-request length and read-response payload length fields support zero through four thousand ninety-six bytes. The compressed format, indicated by the address-compression field set to one, supports a twelve-bit request length ranging from zero through four thousand ninety-five.

A payload of four thousand ninety-six bytes therefore needs the uncompressed address format, with the compression field set to zero. It adds four bytes of overhead, described as about one tenth of one percent in the specification's example. The smaller format cannot represent that length simply by reusing its maximum code.

There is another reason to use the uncompressed form. The compressed form reuses the extension-header length from the preceding uncompressed transaction in the packet. If a different extension-header length is needed, use the uncompressed form to establish it.

Keep these AXI rules in their own section context. The earlier scope table states a two-hundred-fifty-six-byte maximum transaction data size. The specification also gives this four-kilobyte AXI mapping. We retain both statements and don't invent a universal reconciliation.

For a concrete transaction, check its address range, its length, and its required extension-header state. Those checks tell you whether the chosen encoding is valid.

slides.title: Preserve the Interface’s Actual Guarantees
items: Keep command, management, and network responsibilities distinct.
Map identity reversibly and configure opaque AxUSER width.
Reject unsupported noncontiguous WSTRB patterns.
Preserve separate same-AxID read and write order.
Use ac=0 where length or extension-header state requires it.
slides.transcript:
The interface mapping has several independent constraints. The command, management, and Ethernet paths have different roles, and optional management-packet transport is unreliable.

The AXI mapping uses a sixty-bit address, a configured identifier width, and explicitly configured opaque user state. Identifier-to-context mapping is reversible. Enabled write-strobe bytes must be contiguous.

Ordering is separate for reads and writes within an identifier. Neither a shared identifier nor ordered packet delivery provides a universal cross-operation memory order.

Finally, check the encoding boundaries. Four thousand ninety-six bytes needs the uncompressed address format. A changed extension-header length also needs that format, and bursts must respect the four-kilobyte address boundary. Carry those concrete constraints into the completion case in the next module.

choices.feedback_incorrect: The specification guarantees separate same-AxID order within reads and within writes. It does not guarantee read/write cross-ordering, cross-AxID order, or global visibility from the identifier alone.

questions.feedback_correct: The specification guarantees separate same-AxID order within reads and within writes. It does not guarantee read/write cross-ordering, cross-AxID order, or global visibility from the identifier alone.

questions.prompt: Which are valid AXI integration rules? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Configure the number of used AxUSER bits explicitly.
Use ac=0 for a 4096-byte payload.
Use a contiguous range of enabled WSTRB bytes.
Use ac=1 to establish a different extension-header length.

questions.feedback_incorrect: AxUSER width is configured, WSTRB must be contiguous, and 4096B requires ac=0. A changed extension-header length also requires ac=0 because ac=1 reuses the preceding length.

slides.transcript:
Check the interface contract before moving to completion. The first question asks what order a shared AxID actually guarantees. The second asks you to identify valid mapping and encoding rules.

Submit both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required; feedback and retry are available. As you review an answer, separate the identity mapping, the ordering domain, the byte-enable constraint, and the compressed-format limit. Each controls a different part of the integration.

slides.title: Define the Completion Contract Next
slides.next_module_title: Define Completion and Evaluate the Design
slides.transcript:
Thank you for completing Map the XPU Interface to the Transport. You've identified the command and network boundaries, the reversible identity mapping, and the AXI ordering and encoding constraints.

The next module asks when a write is considered complete. We'll compare four possible contracts and work through a write followed by a read. Use the LMS syllabus to open the next module. Keep the mapping facts available; we'll use them to explain the completion case.

modules.title: Define Completion and Evaluate the Design
modules.subtitle: Visibility, errors, cleanup, and a worked AXI write.

slides.title: Define Completion and Evaluate the Design
slides.subtitle: Completion, visibility, errors, and the worked integration case
slides.transcript:
A successful write response can confirm different events depending on the implementation's completion contract. This module makes that choice explicit.

You'll compare completion at memory with earlier queue-acceptance points, then apply the distinction to an aligned write and a following read. We'll also connect the response to error reporting and resource cleanup. The goal is to explain what the application can conclude when success is reported.

slides.title: Completion Choices You Will Evaluate
objectives: Compare completion points and their visibility/error consequences.
Apply encoding and ordering constraints to a 4096B AXI write.
Explain the remaining response/ACK obligation for initiator cleanup.
Evaluate implementation features against the workload contract.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to compare the four write-completion alternatives described in the specification and identify which parts of the path each response covers.

You'll also apply the encoding and ordering constraints to an aligned four-kilobyte write. That case asks whether a following read using the same Advanced eXtensible Interface, or AXI, identifier can rely on ordering, and whether an early queue-completion response establishes observer-visible memory placement.

Finally, you'll explain why the initiator still needs a response or acknowledgement to release outstanding transaction resources. These decisions connect the accelerator's application requirements to the buffering, state, and feature choices inside Scale-Up Ethernet Transport, or SUE-T.

slides.title: Define Exactly When a Write Completes

figure.alt: Four alternative completion points cover different amounts of the write path. Earlier completion changes visibility and error coverage.
figure.caption: Four alternative completion points cover different amounts of the write path. Earlier completion changes visibility and error coverage.

entries.text: Cases restart visibly; they are alternatives, not four required responses
Write committed to the memory queue
Memory not reached from another observer’s view
Write may not yet have left the source
Completion point changes visibility and error coverage
Response / ACK / NAK still required for initiator resource cleanup

text_inventory.review_method: Previously reviewed media retained; revised transaction-flow sequence re-timed and decoded checkpoints reviewed after narration correction.

slides.transcript:
Follow a write from the initiator's transport queue, through the network and target transport, into the destination memory subsystem. The specification describes four alternative completion contracts along that path.

Begin with the most conservative alternative. Completion covers the full network round trip to destination memory and back. The response guarantees the write reached memory successfully, or reports an error encountered along that full path.

Restart the comparison with completion at the destination memory subsystem's queue. The write has been committed to a queue destined for memory. This preserves order, and the specification notes that there may be no actionable error beyond that point in a given design. Its precise behavior remains implementation-specific.

Restart with completion at the target SUE-T queue destined for the accelerator interface. The write has not yet reached memory from another observer's perspective. Errors further into the accelerator, such as translation errors, may not be reported in that response.

Finally, restart with completion at the initiator's own queue destined for its network port. Success can be reported while the write is still local. Network errors, including a corrupted or lost packet, may not be covered by that early response.

These four completion points are alternatives. A write doesn't produce all four responses. Choosing earlier completion changes what success confirms and which errors it covers. The specification leaves that choice to the implementation.

Every choice still needs resource cleanup. The initiator needs a write response, an acknowledgement, or a negative acknowledgement for the outstanding request. Reporting early application success does not remove that requirement.

slides.title: Queue Acceptance and Observer-Visible Memory Differ

bullets.text: Target-queue acceptance can precede memory placement.
Another observer cannot infer memory visibility from that response alone.
Supported/requested global observability holds the XPU response until data is placed.
ACK mode and completion point must be read together.

figure.alt: A reported queue acceptance and observer-visible memory placement are distinct events.
figure.caption: A reported queue acceptance and observer-visible memory placement are distinct events.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.transcript:
Suppose a target transport reports that it has accepted a write into its queue for the accelerator interface. The response can describe successful queue acceptance even though the data hasn't reached memory yet.

Now place another observer beside the memory system. The observer might access that memory through a different interface. A queue-acceptance response does not, by itself, establish that this observer can already read the new data. The specification explicitly calls out that limitation for the target-queue completion alternative.

Global observability supplies a related condition when it is supported and requested. The accelerator holds its response until the data is placed. Either acknowledgement mode can support that behavior. Operational acknowledgement alone is insufficient evidence that the implementation selected the memory-placement point.

The distinction should appear in the application's completion contract. Which event does a successful response confirm? Which observers and access paths rely on that event? What happens if an error occurs after an early response has been returned?

These are implementation questions, so the answer cannot be inferred simply from the presence of a write-response channel or a familiar transport name. The chosen response point must match the behavior the application needs.

Use the queue and memory boundaries as separate facts in the design review. That makes it possible to evaluate a latency optimization without accidentally treating acceptance as a guarantee about all subsequent observation.

slides.title: Apply the Contract to an Aligned 4096-Byte Write

figure.alt: Apply the constraints to an aligned 4096B write and a same-AxID read with target-queue completion. Predict encoding, ordering, and visibility.
figure.caption: Apply the constraints to an aligned 4096B write and a same-AxID read with target-queue completion. Predict encoding, ordering, and visibility.

text_inventory.review_method: Source media inspected; generated video states visually reviewed and checked against decoded checkpoints.

slides.subtitle: Pause the narration to predict each outcome, then resume for the explanation.
slides.transcript:
Work through a concrete integration case. An application issues a four-thousand-ninety-six-byte write aligned to a four-kilobyte boundary. Its enabled write-strobe bytes are contiguous. A following read uses the same AxID. The implementation reports write completion at the target SUE-T queue.

First, choose the request encoding. The compressed address format cannot represent a length of four thousand ninety-six bytes, so use the uncompressed format with address compression set to zero. The aligned write stays within one four-kilobyte boundary. The contiguous byte enables satisfy the write-strobe constraint.

Second, evaluate the ordering assumption. Sharing the identifier does not guarantee ordering between the write and the read. The specification orders reads with reads and writes with writes separately. The application needs an additional established mechanism for any cross-operation dependency; this example does not invent one.

Third, interpret the successful write response. Target-queue completion reports acceptance into the queue for the accelerator interface. It does not establish that another observer can already read the updated data from memory. It may also omit downstream accelerator errors from that early response.

Finally, account for resources. The initiator still needs the write response or an acknowledgement result to clean up the outstanding request's transport resources. Application-facing early success and transport cleanup remain distinct responsibilities.

This case uses the AXI section's four-kilobyte mapping. Keep the earlier two-hundred-fifty-six-byte scope statement separate; the case doesn't resolve that source distinction. The learning outcome is to name the encoding, ordering, completion, and cleanup conclusions individually.

slides.title: Preserve Error Reporting and Initiator Cleanup
rows: Write response or ACK/NAK remains required
slides.transcript:
The response carries information that the source needs to complete the AXI transaction. The interface mapping connects AXI response codes to the semantic response codes used by the transport.

An AXI OKAY response maps to the successful return code. A subordinate error maps to vendor-defined return-code entry zero in the specified mapping, and a decode error maps to vendor-defined return-code entry one. EXOKAY is not supported. Keep this concrete mapping separate from an assumption that every possible AXI behavior is directly provided by the minimal interface.

The completion point determines which path has been covered when that response is produced. A destination-memory completion can cover errors along the full round trip. A target-queue completion may omit accelerator-side errors that occur later. An initiator-queue completion may omit later network errors as well.

The specification leaves the selection mechanism implementation-specific. It may be a static mode or use the delivery-complete field where appropriate, but SUE-T does not define one universal selector for all four alternatives.

Whatever optimization the implementation chooses, a write response or ACK or NACK is still needed to clean up outstanding resources at the initiator. Reporting early success to an application doesn't permit the transport to forget the request without that defined cleanup result.

For a design review, ask for the response-code mapping, the completion point, the errors that can be reported there, and the later cleanup path. Those four answers give the word success a precise meaning.

slides.title: Choose Features Against Your Workload

cards.title: Operation coverage
cards.body: Write/non-fetching atomic simplicity versus read/fetching-atomic capability.

cards.title: Buffering
cards.body: Area cost versus opportunity to pack available work.

cards.title: Transport replay
cards.body: Retained state for recovery versus fatal-loss consequence.

cards.title: ACK mode
cards.body: Delivery state simplicity versus operational response compression.

cards.title: Connection contexts
cards.body: Dedicated state versus dynamic allocation at scale.

slides.transcript:
The specification presents implementation choices that trade endpoint area and state against capability and wire efficiency. Start with the operation set. Supporting only writes and non-fetching atomics can simplify the implementation. Reads and fetching atomics add functionality and data-bearing responses.

Next, consider transmit buffering. More buffering can increase opportunities to pack commands that are already available together. Less buffering saves area but reduces those opportunities. The scheduler's work-conserving rule still applies; a larger buffer doesn't authorize waiting just to fill a packet.

Transport retransmission adds retained data and state for recovery. Removing it makes a lost packet fatal to the connection. Delivery acknowledgement needs less managed operation state, while Operational acknowledgement can improve wire efficiency by retaining state and compressing successful data-free responses.

In its packed-operation example over the Unified Forwarding Header, or UFH, with sixteen-bit addresses, the specification reports wire efficiency greater than ninety percent for Operational acknowledgement. It compares that with less than eighty percent for Delivery acknowledgement using a sixteen-byte response command. Keep those conditions attached to the percentages. They aren't a universal throughput guarantee across all workloads and formats.

Finally, dedicated versus dynamic delivery contexts changes the state required at scale. The examples called SUE-lite and SUE-full combine some of these choices. SUE-lite uses no transport retransmission, link-layer retry, writes only, and Delivery acknowledgement. SUE-full uses retransmission, Operational acknowledgement, and dynamic contexts. They are examples of feature combinations, not mandatory product categories.

Select a combination by stating the workload's operations, latency, visibility, resilience, and scale requirements. Then review the implementation's specific choices against those requirements.

slides.title: Make the Completion Assumptions Explicit
items: Name the event that a successful write response confirms.
Separate queue acceptance from observer-visible memory.
Account for ordering and encoding independently.
Preserve initiator response/ACK cleanup obligations.
Evaluate feature combinations against explicit workload requirements.
slides.transcript:
An implementation's completion contract connects reported success to a specific event. The four write-completion alternatives cover different portions of the path, from destination memory back to the initiator's local queue.

Earlier completion can reduce what the response establishes about memory visibility and error coverage. A shared AxID does not fill in missing read/write cross-ordering. An encoding choice does not choose the completion event.

The initiator still needs the response or acknowledgement result that cleans up the outstanding request. Treat that obligation separately from any early application-facing success.

Finally, choose the operation set, buffers, retransmission, acknowledgement mode, and connection allocation against the workload's actual requirements. The specification's examples help frame those choices; the implementation needs to make its own contract clear.

slides.transcript:
Before finishing, check how you interpret success. The first question asks what target-queue completion establishes. The second asks you to identify valid conclusions about errors, cleanup, and feature combinations.

Submit both questions once to continue. Correct answers aren't required, and you can retry after feedback. Use the explanation to connect each claim to a boundary in the write path. Being able to name that boundary is the practical skill this module has been building.

slides.transcript:
Thank you for completing all four modules of Ethernet Transport for XPU Scale-Up Systems.

You can now trace a transaction, explain packing and ordered recovery, and review the accelerator interface's completion contract. Use those skills to ask precise questions about a real endpoint: what is guaranteed, at which boundary, under which configuration? Keep the SUE-T Base Specification available as you apply the learning to your next design or implementation review.

term_glossary.tooltip: Traffic class: independent traffic grouping; requests and responses use different TCs to avoid deadlock.
Command Payload Data Unit: a mapped command and its associated data before packet assembly.
Packet Sequence Number: connection state used to track the expected packet and acknowledgements.
Packet Delivery Context: a tracked connection with sequence, acknowledgement, and timeout state.
Reliable Ordered Delivery for Local networks: the UET packet-reliability protocol used by SUE-T.
aliases: Reliable Ordered Delivery for Local networks

term_glossary.tooltip: Acknowledges delivery to the destination XPU; the XPU response travels independently.
Associates the destination XPU response with the request; can compress successful data-free responses.
When supported and requested, holds the XPU response until the data is placed.
Negative acknowledgement sent for an unexpected packet sequence; later arrivals are dropped until the expected packet arrives.
Optional retransmission that replays from the missing point in an ordered packet sequence.
Link Layer Retransmission: link-level retry, distinct from optional transport GoBackN recovery.
Priority Flow Control: one permitted mechanism for required lossless service on SUE-T traffic classes.
Credit-Based Flow Control: one permitted mechanism for required lossless service on SUE-T traffic classes.
Advanced eXtensible Interface: the read/write interface used by the specification’s example integration mapping.
AXI identifier: maps reversibly to PDCID; same-ID reads and writes are ordered separately.
Opaque application state carried unchanged; used width is configured to 0, 32, 64, or 128 bits.
Write strobe: enabled bytes must form a contiguous range; unsupported masks are local errors.

lms_short_description: Trace transactions, explain reliable delivery, and define accelerator completion contracts.
lms_long_description:
Learn how SUE-T v1.0.0 carries accelerator memory transactions over an Ethernet scale-up fabric. Trace command mapping and acknowledgements, predict packet packing and recovery, map XPU and AXI interfaces, and compare completion points, memory visibility, and error handling. This intermediate technical course includes narrated slides, six synchronized teaching videos, worked examples, and knowledge checks. Allow about 75 minutes, including practice and review.

Module 1: From XPU Transactions to Ethernet Transport — about 18 minutes. Endpoint scope, transaction flow, ACK modes, and visibility.
Module 2: Efficient Packets on a Lossless Fabric — about 25 minutes. Queue service, packing limits, PDC state, and lossless reliability.
Module 3: Map the XPU Interface to the Transport — about 16 minutes. Command/network roles, identity, ordering, and encoding.
Module 4: Define Completion and Evaluate the Design — about 16 minutes. Visibility, errors, cleanup, and a worked AXI write.
